power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective:
To compare LLM and prompting strategies for labeling Specific Incidental Findings (SIFs) occurring during lung cancer screening, in radiology reports.

In November 2022, the Council of the European Union (EU) recommended EU countries to explore the feasibility and effectiveness of Lung Cancer Screening (LCS) with use of low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). [1] Beyond the primary purpose of early detection of lung cancer, LDCT imaging may reveal a variety of incidental findings (IFs).
text.formatted: In November 2022, the Council of the European Union (EU) recommended EU countries to explore the feasibility and effectiveness of Lung Cancer Screening (LCS) with use of low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> Beyond the primary purpose of early detection of lung cancer, LDCT imaging may reveal a variety of incidental findings (IFs).

text.text: A group of six European radiological societies published a statement about the management of IFs for LCS. [2] The statement paper named nine specific incidental findings (SIFs): aortic valve disease (AVD), bronchiectasis (Bron), consolidation (Cons), coronary artery calcification (CAC), emphysema (Emp), interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA), mediastinal mass (MM), mediastinal lymph nodes (MLN) and thyroid abnormalities (TA).
text.formatted: A group of six European radiological societies published a statement about the management of IFs for LCS. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> The statement paper named nine specific incidental findings (SIFs): aortic valve disease (AVD), bronchiectasis (Bron), consolidation (Cons), coronary artery calcification (CAC), emphysema (Emp), interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA), mediastinal mass (MM), mediastinal lymph nodes (MLN) and thyroid abnormalities (TA).

text.text: The implementation of LCS across the EU has several challenges, including the anticipated workload for radiologists to read the large volume of LDCT scans.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms could support by assisting the interpretation of LDCT scans.
Despite more than 15 CE-marked commercial solutions for pulmonary nodules in Europe, [3] the development of AI algorithms for SIFs is still in its infancy.
text.formatted: Despite more than 15 CE-marked commercial solutions for pulmonary nodules in Europe, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> the development of AI algorithms for SIFs is still in its infancy.

text.text: A large amount of annotated SIFs from retrospective CT scans are needed to train a SIF detection and classification algorithm.

However, screening programs such as the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) lack comprehensive annotations for SIFs, [4] they only include optional verbatim fields and a few were encoded during screening, namely: consolidation and emphysema.

text.text: By extracting SIFs from the clinical text, radiology reports can serve as weak supervision for training models that can classify SIFs in CT scans.

This process enables the creation of large labeled datasets that do not require time-intensive manual annotations. [6] Traditional keyword search methods fail to effectively capture the nuances of medical reports, as they often miss context, cannot handle negation well and struggle with clinical terminology variations.

text.text: At present, no publicly available Natural Language Processing (NLP) model exists for labelling the SIFs in LCS from CT reports, such as CheXpert/CheXbert which labels 13 findings in chest X-ray reports. Bhayana et al. 2024 demonstrated the potential of zero-shot prompting GPT-4 for identifying incidental findings in radiology reports, however there is a growing demand to validate light weight, privacy-preserving, open-source models for CT report labeling. [7] Besides model choice, prompting engineering influences LLM performance. Wei et al. 2022 introduced Chain of Thought (CoT) Prompting to encourage LLMs to think step by step to improve performance on reasoning tasks. [8] Prior research in CoT prompting in radiology by Khosravi et al. 2025 found variable effects depending on the model, and so more investigation is needed to determine if CoT is a recommended strategy in radiology. [9] Objective Our aim is to investigate the best strategy for the automatic labelling of radiology reports for SIFs defined during LCS.

text.text: This retrospective study was designed to determine the feasibility and best strategy of LLMs to annotate radiology reports for SIFs.

text.text: For this study, we used an existing dataset consisting of all Dutch CT thorax abdomen radiology reports between 13 th May 1997 and 1 st February 2021, previously downloaded from the electronic health record (EHR) system of our institution.
The reports were de-identified using an internal radiology report anonymization method that was approved by the local institutional privacy office.

We applied the following exclusion criteria to the initial pool of radiology reports; patients aged less than 18, post-mortem, punction, pediatric, drainage, radiofrequency ablation (RFA), or external studies.
After applying the exclusion criteria, 200 reports were randomly selected from the time period: 1 st of January 2016 and the 1 st December 2017.
This dataset was then extended to increase the diversity of the dataset with 100 reports, which were randomly selected from entire date range 13 th May 1997 and 1 st February 2021.

Prior to sending radiology reports to external cloud services, they were manually checked for remaining presence of personal health information, and if needed remaining personal health information was removed, according to hospital privacy regulations.
A quality check was performed on the selected reports, more details can be found in Supplementary Information S1.
No pre-processing of the radiology report was done, the full report was used, more details can be found in Supplementary Information S2.
The reference standard for presence of SIFs was set by a general radiologist (E.T.S.) with 32 years of experience.
The radiologist was provided with the IF statement paper, [2] and was asked to label the presence or absence of the nine SIFs following the statement paper recommendations.
text.formatted: The radiologist was provided with the IF statement paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> and was asked to label the presence or absence of the nine SIFs following the statement paper recommendations.

text.text: The software used for labeling was Microsoft Excel (v2408) and Doccano (v1.8.4). [10] The following SIFs were annotated: aortic valve disease (AVD), bronchiectasis (Bron), consolidation (Cons), coronary artery calcification (CAC), emphysema (Emph), interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA), abnormalities in mediastinal lymph nodes (MLN), mediastinal mass (MM) and thyroid abnormalities (TA).
text.formatted: The software used for labeling was Microsoft Excel (v2408) and Doccano (v1.8.4). <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> The following SIFs were annotated: aortic valve disease (AVD), bronchiectasis (Bron), consolidation (Cons), coronary artery calcification (CAC), emphysema (Emph), interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA), abnormalities in mediastinal lymph nodes (MLN), mediastinal mass (MM) and thyroid abnormalities (TA).

text.text: Four LLMs were evaluated in this study; two proprietary models: GPT-5, [11] and GPT-4-Turbo model, [12] via the OpenAI API, and two open-source models: Llama-3.1-8B-INST by Meta, [13] and MedGemma-4B-IT by Google. [14] As a baseline comparison, we developed a Keyword Search (regex) to also label the reports for the nine SIFs.
text.formatted: Four LLMs were evaluated in this study; two proprietary models: GPT-5, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> and GPT-4-Turbo model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> via the OpenAI API, and two open-source models: Llama-3.1-8B-INST by Meta, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and MedGemma-4B-IT by Google. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> As a baseline comparison, we developed a Keyword Search (regex) to also label the reports for the nine SIFs.

text.text: The open-source models were deployed and run locally, further information about the labelling methods can be found in the Supplementary Information S3 and S4.
Four different prompting strategies were applied in this study.

The first prompting strategy was a general prompt which instructed the LLM to label the report for all nine SIFs, and did not offer any detail regarding how to determine their presence or absence (Prompt V1).

The second strategy divided the prompt per SIF and instructed the LLM to label the report only for the presence or absence of a single SIF, and offered additional information based on the IF Statement paper, [2] to determine the presence or absence of the SIF (Prompt V2).
text.formatted: The second strategy divided the prompt per SIF and instructed the LLM to label the report only for the presence or absence of a single SIF, and offered additional information based on the IF Statement paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> to determine the presence or absence of the SIF (Prompt V2).

text.text: The third strategy was the same as the second, only it added CoT (Prompt V3).
The fourth strategy was the same as the third, but few shot examples were also provided; three examples consisting each of a radiology report, reasoning, and output were provided (Prompt V4).
More details on the prompting strategies can be found in the Supplementary Information S5.

text.text: Post processing of the output of the models was performed to extract scores, more details can be found in Supplementary Information S6.
Cohen's Kappa was the primary metric used to assess the agreement between the automatic methods and the radiologist.

The Cohen's Kappa was interpreted into these agreement categorizations: no agreement (κ < 0), slight agreement (κ: 0.0 -0.20), fair agreement (κ: 0.21 -0.40), moderate agreement (κ: 0.41 -0.60), substantial agreement (κ: 0.61 -0.80), and almost perfect agreement (κ: 0.81 -1.00) as suggested by Landis and Koch (1977). [15] Supporting metrics include sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score.

text.text: All 95% confidence intervals were calculated using bootstrapping with 1000 bootstrap iterations.
In Supplementary Information S7, more details are given regarding how the analysis into the differences between model and prompt types was performed.

text.text: In total, we obtained 264,186 reports from the period 1997 -2021.
After applying our exclusion criteria, 212,017 reports were left for further analysis.
From this set, 300 radiology reports were randomly selected.
As a result of this selection, the date range of these selected 300 reports was between 19 th March 2003 and 28 th December 2020.

text.text: In example report 1, GPT-5 V4 accurately justified labeling ILA as present, whereas in example report 2, GPT-4-Turbo V4 incorrectly used atelectasis as justification for labeling consolidation as present.
In this study, we investigated the best strategy to automatically label specific incidental findings (SIFs) occurring during Lung Cancer Screening (LCS) in CT radiology reports.
This work provides insight into the first step of applying LLM-extracted pseudo-labels for training models to classify SIFs in CT scans.
We compared five labelling methods: four large language models (LLMs) with four different prompting strategies and the Keyword Search method.
We used Cohen's Kappa as the primary evaluation metric.

The secondary classification metrics were largely consistent with the Cohen's κ results, with F1 reproducing the main trends observed across models and prompting strategies, while sensitivity and specificity provided complementary information on the types of classification errors.
We found that there is not a single best strategy for labelling all of the SIFs.
GPT-5 performed better than all other methods for five out of nine of the SIFs.
GPT-4-Turbo performed better than the other models for two of the SIFs.
MedGemma-4B-IT performed better than the other models There are several advantages for using lighter weight, open-source models for medical applications.

Savage at al. 2025 outlined general advantages, such as customizability, flexibility for commercial use, and security -as open-source LLMs can be fully downloaded to run locally on-site or in institutionally managed cloud instances. [19] In terms of size, running smaller models requires less resources to run and this translates to lower cost, greater portability, and lower environmental impact.
text.formatted: Savage at al. 2025 outlined general advantages, such as customizability, flexibility for commercial use, and security -as open-source LLMs can be fully downloaded to run locally on-site or in institutionally managed cloud instances. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> In terms of size, running smaller models requires less resources to run and this translates to lower cost, greater portability, and lower environmental impact.

text.text: In this study, we have demonstrated that for labelling some of the SIFs, lighter weight open-source methods offered better, or comparable performance to proprietary, heavier models.
However, we found that the light-weight open-source models were more affected by prompt engineering than the proprietary models.

Smaller models may be more affected by prompt engineering because they have less representational capacity (lower capabilities to fill in missing context from the prompt) and they are fine-tuned on small instruction datasets with limited prompt diversity.
Our results demonstrated that CoT prompting yielded lower agreement with the radiologist.

Khosravi et al. 2025 also found that CoT led to poorer results for smaller models for determining the presence or absence of a finding in radiology reports. [9] They hypothesized that due to model 'overthinking', performance on simple tasks is reduced, and concluded that prompting strategy should be task specific.
text.formatted: Khosravi et al. 2025 also found that CoT led to poorer results for smaller models for determining the presence or absence of a finding in radiology reports. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> They hypothesized that due to model 'overthinking', performance on simple tasks is reduced, and concluded that prompting strategy should be task specific.

text.text: For both the open-source and the proprietary models we found that sometimes the reasoning output for a label was nonsensical.
For example, GPT-4-Turbo/Prompt V4 wrongly justified labelling presence for consolidation because the report mentioned atelectasis.
In many reports consolidation and atelectasis are often named together and pre-training on such reports may have resulted in this misunderstanding.
Another example, MedGemma-4B-IT/Prompt V3 incorrectly labelled for the presence of AVD when the report only referenced the aortic arch.
In this work, we did not find an improvement in agreement when few shot examples were provided in the CoT (Prompt V4).

This result was similarly found by Nowak et al. 2025, and they speculated that examples led some LLMs to allocate less attention to the instruction part of the prompt. [16] In longer prompts, LLMs tend to focus on information at the beginning and end of the instructions, and that performance reduces when models must access relevant information in the middle of prompts. [20] This may suggest that CoT is better suited for tasks with shorter examples, rather than for our task which required the entire radiology report as an example.

text.text: There are several limitations to this study.
Firstly, the size of our dataset (300 reports) resulted in only five examples of mediastinal mass.
While in a screening setting the prevalence of mediastinal mass would be very low, this small number reduces the certainty of our conclusions regarding mediastinal mass.
Given that it took the radiologist about two hours to label 100 reports, for feasibility purposes 300 reports were selected.
An extensive analysis using a larger corpus of reports would help future studies to guarantee a substantial number of cases for each SIF.
Secondly, a single radiologist served as the reference standard.

As inter-reader agreement was not assessed, we cannot determine whether disagreement between the models and the reference labels reflects label noise, model limitations or intrinsic reader variability.
Future work should include multiple readers and report human-human agreement.

Thirdly, we investigated only the labelling of Dutch radiology reports from a single center, therefore the generalizability of the results to other centers with other languages should be investigated in future studies.
Additionally, as this was an exploratory investigation which evaluated the agreement between the models and a radiologist, the statistical significance of differences between models was not computed.
Furthermore, the prompt experiment of few shot learning without CoT was not included in this study, limiting our conclusions regarding the influence of few shot learning.
In this study, a variety of LLMs in terms of model size, proprietary status, release date are used.
We acknowledge that this field is rapidly evolving and that these evaluations are inherently time dependent, and may not fully reflect the performance of future LLMs.
In conclusion, this study evaluated the best strategy of using large language models to automatically label lung cancer screening-relevant incidental findings in Dutch radiology reports.
LLMs reached moderate or above agreement with a radiologist for labelling radiology reports for SIFs.
For five out of the nine SIFs, open-source lighter LLMs had comparable or higher agreement with a radiologist than proprietary, heavier LLMs.
There was not one optimal model/prompt strategy across SIFs, and CoT-prompting reduced performance.
GPT-5 reached almost perfect agreement for most SIFs, while MedGemma-4B-IT demonstrated substantial or above performance for most SIFs.
These results support using LLM-based report labeling as a weak-annotation approach to help scale training data for future incidental finding algorithms.
For future weakly supervised labeling pipelines, we suggest starting with concise non-CoT prompts and if privacy is essential: lightweight open-source models.
We recommend selecting the optimal model and prompt separately for each finding using an expert labelled validation dataset, before being deployed to generate large-scale pseudo-labels.
